research.subtitle: The interdependence of shipping lines and island nations — the cases of Madagascar and Mauritius
research.methodology: Mixed methodology applied to a comparative study of Madagascar and Mauritius: literature review, analysis of connectivity and logistics-performance data (UNCTAD Liner Shipping Connectivity Index, World Bank Logistics Performance Index) and interviews.

toc.part: Part I — Theoretical framework: sea power, dependence and logistics power
chapters: 1.1 The sea as the historical foundation of world trade
1.2 From states' sea power to the sea power of private carriers
1.3 Defining maritime dependence: asymmetry, substitution and logistics sovereignty
1.4 Logistics capitalism, economic dependence and neo-colonisation: secondary frameworks
1.5 Research propositions and comparative analytical grid

toc.part: Part II — Comparative study: Madagascar and Mauritius facing island maritime dependence
chapters: 2.2 Comparative results: connectivity, logistics performance, absorption capacity, crises, the state's role
3.1 For Madagascar: building a better-steered maritime dependence
3.2 For Mauritius: consolidating a better-organised maritime dependence
3.4 Limits of the recommendations and future research directions

summary: The thesis analyses the maritime dependence of island states on international logistics companies, and how that dependence shapes their commercial competitiveness, economic sovereignty and negotiating capacity.
It rests on a comparative study of Madagascar and Mauritius, combining a literature review, connectivity and logistics-performance data (UNCTAD and World Bank indices) and interviews.

It concludes that island states' maritime dependence is structural and often asymmetric, but that it plays out as much internally — port organisation, data quality, coordination of actors — as externally.

Logistics sovereignty is defined not as an exit from interdependence but as a state's capacity to know, measure and steer its dependence; the recommendations include a national flows observatory, a total-landed-cost approach and regional maritime diversification.
